subject: HSS
overview: Teach HSS through stories, primary-source photos, maps, and hands-on projects. Use 'See, Think, Wonder' with every photo and document, connect each topic to your child's own family and community, and let them explain ideas aloud before writing. Preview the read-aloud books — several touch on history topics like segregation and immigration that may prompt questions — and answer honestly at a first-grade level.

weeks.prep: A simple board game, chart paper and markers, picture cards of community signs (stop sign, crosswalk, library 'quiet,' park rules), and 'What If Everybody Did That?' by Ellen Javernick (library).
misconceptions: Thinking rules are only to keep kids from having fun: show how rules keep people safe and make things fair.
Thinking rules only exist at home or school: point out community rules (traffic signs, park hours).
Confusing rights with doing whatever you want: rights come with responsibilities.

days.guide: Play a board game for two minutes with no rules (anyone can move anywhere). Then stop and ask what went wrong and why rules matter.

questions.a: Answers vary: arguing, confusion, unfair play, no one knew who won.
To make play fair and help everyone know what to do.

days.guide: Walk the neighborhood. Your child draws or photographs 5 signs and says what each keeps safe.

questions.q: What does a stop sign keep safe?
questions.a: Drivers, walkers, and bikers — cars stop so no one crashes.
To show people a safe place to cross where drivers expect them.

days.guide: Write 5 home/homeschool rules together and illustrate each.

questions.q: Give a good home rule and its reason.
questions.a: Example: Put toys away — so no one trips and things don't get lost.
Everyone in the family.

days.guide: Read 'What If Everybody Did That?' and match 3 rights with 3 responsibilities.

questions.q: What does the book ask about small actions like dropping litter?
questions.a: What would happen if everybody did that — small actions add up to big problems.

questions.q: Match: the right to use the park.
questions.a: Responsibility to keep it clean.

days.guide: Your child explains one home rule and one community rule and what could happen without each.

questions.q: What would happen without traffic lights?
questions.a: Cars could crash and people could get hurt.

questions.q: Why do we have a rule to wash hands before eating?
questions.a: To keep germs away so we don't get sick.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = states a home rule and a community rule, explains the purpose of each (safety, fairness, order), and what could happen without it; 3 = two rules with one clear purpose; 2 = names rules without purposes; 1 = cannot name a rule.

weeks.prep: 'The Golden Rule' by Ilene Cooper (library), role-play cards (someone cuts in line; a friend is left out; someone takes your toy; a sibling is sad), and a kindness log (paper with 3 boxes).
misconceptions: Thinking the Golden Rule means 'do what others do to you': it means treat others the way you want to be treated.
Thinking disagreeing is always rude: you can disagree politely and respectfully.
Thinking kindness must be big: small acts (holding a door, sharing) count.

days.guide: Read 'The Golden Rule.' Your child says the rule in their own words.

questions.a: Treat others the way you want to be treated.

questions.q: According to the book, is the Golden Rule found in only one religion or culture?
questions.a: No — versions of it are found in many religions and cultures around the world.

days.guide: Act out 4 situations and show a Golden Rule choice for each.

questions.q: A friend is left out of a game. What's a Golden Rule choice?
questions.a: Invite them to join.

questions.q: Someone cuts in line. What can you do?
questions.a: Calmly say 'The line starts back there, please,' or tell an adult.

days.guide: Survey family on favorite food; practice saying 'I see it differently because...' politely.

questions.q: Your brother says pizza is the best food; you like tacos. What can you say?
questions.a: 'I see it differently because I like tacos more.'

questions.q: Is it okay to have different opinions?
questions.a: Yes, as long as we're respectful.

days.guide: Your child does 3 kind acts this week and draws each in the log.

questions.a: Example: helping set the table, sharing a toy.

questions.q: How do kind acts follow the Golden Rule?
questions.a: We're kind because we'd like others to be kind to us.

days.guide: Your child draws a comic strip of someone following the Golden Rule and explains it.

questions.a: Example: A girl shares her snack with a boy who forgot his, because she'd want help if she forgot hers.

questions.q: Why is that the Golden Rule?
questions.a: She treats him the way she'd want to be treated.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = comic clearly shows a Golden Rule choice and explanation names how the character treats someone the way they'd want to be treated; 3 = clear comic, partial explanation; 2 = comic unclear; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: A simple outdoor game (tag, kickball) or board game, scenario cards (fair/unfair), and a T-chart (Good Sport / Poor Sport).
misconceptions: Thinking 'fair' always means 'exactly the same': fair means everyone gets what they need (e.g., glasses for someone who can't see).
Thinking good sports only win: good sportsmanship is how you act whether you win or lose.
Bragging when winning: say 'good game' and thank the other player.

days.guide: Discuss whether fair always means the same. Sort scenario cards into fair and unfair.

questions.q: Is it fair if only one child gets to choose the game every day?
questions.a: No — taking turns is fair.

questions.q: Is it fair that a child who needs glasses gets them and others don't?
questions.a: Yes — fair means getting what you need.

days.guide: Play a backyard game; practice taking turns, following rules, and shaking hands at the end.

questions.q: What do you say at the end of a game?
questions.a: 'Good game!'
So everyone gets a chance.

days.guide: Role-play good and poor ways to win and lose. Fill a T-chart of sportsmanlike words.

questions.a: 'Good game, you played well.'
Yelling, quitting, bragging, or blaming others.

days.guide: Your child writes and signs a 3-line good-sport pledge.

questions.a: I will follow the rules.
I will say 'good game' whether I win or lose.

days.guide: Your child tells how a good sport acted in a game this week.

questions.q: How did you act like a good sport?
questions.a: Answers vary — e.g., I took turns and congratulated my sister.

questions.q: What does a good sport do if a game feels unfair?
questions.a: Calmly talk about it or ask an adult.

weeks.assessment_key: T-chart: proficient lists at least 3 good-sport words/actions (take turns, follow rules, say 'good game,' encourage others) and 3 poor-sport ones (cheat, brag, quit, yell). Pledge: 3 positive lines, signed.

weeks.prep: 'Duck for President' by Doreen Cronin (library), paper ballots, a box for a ballot box, and a tally chart.
misconceptions: Thinking the majority means everyone agrees: some people still voted for the other choice.
Thinking voting is only for presidents: we can vote in families and clubs.
Thinking the losing side should sulk: we respect the result.

days.guide: Read 'Duck for President.' Talk about why the animals voted.

questions.q: Why did Duck want an election?
questions.a: He was tired of doing chores for Farmer Brown and wanted to be in charge.

questions.q: What did Duck learn about being a leader?
questions.a: Running things (the farm, the state, the country) was hard work, so he went back to the farm.

days.guide: Hold a family vote on Friday's movie or snack with paper ballots. Count tallies.

questions.a: Everyone voted, and we counted the votes.
So people can vote how they want without pressure.

days.guide: Count votes; explain that the most votes wins; discuss feelings.

questions.q: Popcorn 3 votes, fruit 2 votes. Which wins?
questions.a: Popcorn.

questions.q: How should the fruit voters act?
questions.a: Accept the result kindly; there will be other votes.

days.guide: Propose a new household rule and let everyone vote.

questions.q: What happens if the rule gets more yes votes than no?
questions.a: It becomes a rule.
Yes — everyone votes on the rule.

days.guide: Your child explains direct democracy in one sentence and gives the example.

questions.a: Everyone votes directly on a decision or rule.
Our family voted on the Friday movie.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: proficient = 'In direct democracy, everyone votes on the decision' plus an accurate example (e.g., the family movie vote where the choice with the most votes won).

weeks.prep: Your city's website or newspaper (to find mayor and city council), paper for campaign posters, two stuffed animals, and ballots.
misconceptions: Thinking leaders can make any rule they want: they must follow laws and voters can choose new leaders.
Mixing up direct and representative democracy: direct = everyone votes on the rule; representative = people elect leaders who make rules.
Thinking only adults' voices matter: kids can share ideas with leaders by writing letters.

days.guide: Explain that in big places, people elect a small group (city council, mayor) to make rules for everyone.

questions.a: A person elected to make decisions for a group of people.

questions.q: Why can't everyone in a city vote on every rule?
questions.a: There are too many people and too many rules.

days.guide: Look up your mayor and city council; find one rule they made.

questions.a: Name from city website.
Examples: park hours, speed limits, leash laws, recycling rules.

days.guide: Make campaign posters for two stuffed-animal candidates; hold an election for 'family representative.'

questions.q: What does a campaign poster tell?
questions.a: The candidate's name and what they promise to do.
The voters (family).

days.guide: Make a T-chart comparing direct and representative democracy.

questions.a: Family votes on a movie.
City council makes a park rule after people elect them.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 assessment.

questions.q: People elect a mayor. Direct or representative?
questions.a: Representative.
Treat others the way you want to be treated.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test (suggested): Sort — 1) Family votes on dinner: direct 2) Voters elect a mayor who makes rules: representative 3) Class votes on a game: direct 4) City council passes a law: representative 5) Club members vote on a name: direct. 6) Golden Rule: treat others as you want to be treated. 7) Why rules? safety and fairness. Proficient 6–7.

weeks.prep: Blocks or small boxes, a toy, a camera/phone, and paper.
misconceptions: Thinking maps must show everything: maps show the important things from above using symbols.
Drawing a side view instead of bird's-eye view: imagine you're a bird looking straight down.
Thinking a photo and a map are the same: a photo shows what something looks like; a map shows where things are.

days.guide: Look at a toy from above and from the side; draw both.

questions.a: Looking straight down from above.

questions.q: What does a cup look like from above?
questions.a: A circle.

days.guide: Build a 3-D model of your bedroom with blocks and boxes.

questions.q: What could stand for your bed?
questions.a: A rectangular block or box.
A small copy of something real.

days.guide: Photograph the room and compare with the model.

questions.q: What does the photo show that the model doesn't?
questions.a: Real colors, details, objects.

questions.q: What does the model show better?
questions.a: Where things are compared to each other, from any side.

days.guide: Draw a bird's-eye map of the room with simple symbols.

questions.q: How would you draw a bed on the map?
questions.a: A rectangle.

questions.q: How would you draw a round rug?
questions.a: A circle.

days.guide: Your child explains one thing a model shows better and one thing a picture shows better.

questions.a: Where things are in the room and their size from all sides.
Real colors and details.

weeks.assessment_key: Map rubric: 4 = bird's-eye view, main furniture placed correctly with simple symbols, plus clear model-vs-picture comparison; 3 = mostly correct; 2 = side views or major misplacements; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: A compass (or phone compass), sticky notes labeled N, S, E, W, a park map with a key, and a small 'treasure.'
misconceptions: Thinking north is always 'up' in real life: north is a direction; on most maps it's at the top.
Mixing up east and west: 'Never Eat Soggy Waffles' (N, E, S, W clockwise).
Ignoring the map key: the key explains what each symbol means.

days.guide: Use a compass to label walls N, S, E, W. Follow directions like 'take 3 steps north.'

questions.q: What are the four cardinal directions?
questions.a: North, south, east, west.
West.

days.guide: Study a park map's key; find 5 symbols.

questions.a: A box that explains what the symbols mean.

questions.q: What might a tree symbol mean?
questions.a: A wooded area or trees.

days.guide: Draw a compass rose and add it to the room map.

questions.q: What does a compass rose show?
questions.a: Directions (N, S, E, W).

questions.q: Where is north usually on a map?
questions.a: At the top.

days.guide: Follow a family-made map with symbols and directions to find hidden treasure.

questions.q: How did you use the map?
questions.a: Followed symbols and directions.

questions.q: If the map says go east from the couch, which way?
questions.a: Toward the side labeled E.

days.guide: Your child makes a yard/street map with a key of 4 symbols and a compass rose.

questions.a: Answers vary — e.g., house, tree, mailbox, driveway.

questions.q: Where is your house compared to the street?
questions.a: Answers use directions.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = map with 4 symbols explained in a key, compass rose with N/S/E/W correct, and features placed accurately; 3 = one part missing; 2 = no key or compass rose; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Large paper, a printed street map of your area (or online map), colored pencils.
misconceptions: Drawing landmarks in the wrong order along the route: walk or check the online map.
Directions without landmarks: add 'turn left at the park.'
Making the map too small to read: plan space before drawing.

days.guide: Walk your neighborhood and list landmarks.

questions.a: An important or easy-to-see place that helps you find your way.
Example: the library, park, fire station.

days.guide: Find your home on a printed or online map.

questions.q: How did you find your street?
questions.a: By its name on the map.
Answers vary.

days.guide: Draw a community map with home, 4 landmarks, key, compass rose.

questions.a: The symbols for each landmark.

questions.q: Where does the compass rose go?
questions.a: In a corner of the map.

days.guide: Draw a route from home to the library; describe it with directions.

questions.a: Example: Go north on Oak Street, turn east at the park, the library is on the left.
The path you take from one place to another.

days.guide: Your child gives a family member directions to a landmark using the map.

questions.a: Using directions (N/S/E/W), street names, and landmarks.

questions.q: Did the listener reach the landmark?
questions.a: Check by following on the map.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = map with home, 4 landmarks, key, compass rose, and accurate route described with cardinal directions; 3 = one element missing; 2 = route unclear; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: A globe, a U.S. map, a California map, blank outline maps, and paper for nesting circles.
misconceptions: Thinking California is a country: it is a state in the United States.
Thinking the capital is Los Angeles or San Francisco: the capital is Sacramento.
Thinking globes and flat maps show different places: both show Earth; the globe is round like Earth.

days.guide: Make nesting circles: home → city → California → United States → North America → Earth.

questions.q: Which is bigger: California or the United States?
questions.a: The United States.

questions.q: What continent is the U.S. on?
questions.a: North America.

days.guide: Find your city, Sacramento, and the Pacific Ocean on a California map.

questions.a: Sacramento.
The Pacific Ocean.

days.guide: Find California on a U.S. map; name the bordering states.

questions.a: Oregon (north), Nevada (east), Arizona (southeast).

questions.q: What country borders California to the south?
questions.a: Mexico.

days.guide: Find the U.S. and California on a globe; compare to a flat map.

questions.q: How is a globe different from a flat map?
questions.a: A globe is round like Earth; a flat map shows Earth flat.
The globe.

days.guide: Label your city, California, and the U.S. on blank maps.

questions.q: Label California on a U.S. map.
questions.a: On the west coast, along the Pacific.
In northern-central California.

weeks.assessment_key: Labeled maps: proficient = city in the right area of California, Sacramento marked, Pacific Ocean labeled, California correctly shaded on the U.S. map, and the U.S. labeled on a North America/world outline.

weeks.prep: A globe, a world map, paper continent cut-outs, a blue world map outline, animal pictures, and a blank world map.
misconceptions: Thinking there is one big ocean: there are named oceans (Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic, and often the Southern Ocean).
Confusing countries and continents: a continent is a huge land area with many countries.
Mixing up Antarctica and the Arctic: Antarctica is the frozen continent at the bottom (south); the Arctic Ocean is at the top (north).

days.guide: Learn a continents song and point to each continent.

questions.a: North America, South America, Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia, Antarctica.
Asia.

days.guide: Find the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic Oceans; trace them.

questions.a: Pacific.

questions.q: Which ocean is between North America and Europe?
questions.a: Atlantic.

days.guide: Cut out continents and glue them in the right places.

questions.a: Southeast of Asia, between the Indian and Pacific Oceans.

questions.q: What continent is south of North America?
questions.a: South America.

days.guide: Place animals on their continents.

questions.a: Australia.
Antarctica (and other southern lands).
Africa.

days.guide: Your child labels 7 continents and 4 oceans.

questions.q: Which ocean is at the very top of the globe?
questions.a: Arctic.

questions.q: Which continent do we live on?
questions.a: North America.

weeks.assessment_key: Labeling key: North America, South America, Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia, Antarctica; Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic Oceans (Southern Ocean accepted if added). Proficient 10–11 of 11.

weeks.prep: Photos of an igloo, a stilt house, an adobe home, and an apartment (Library of Congress/Smithsonian), clothing cards (snow, rain, hot, desert), and images of California beach, Sierra Nevada, and desert.
misconceptions: Thinking people everywhere live the same way: environment shapes homes, food, clothing, and travel.
Thinking igloos are where most Arctic people live today: they were traditional temporary shelters; most people live in modern houses now.
Judging other ways of life as 'weird': they make sense for the place.

days.guide: Compare homes; tell how each fits its environment.

questions.q: Why are stilt houses on stilts?
questions.a: To stay above floods, water, or wet ground.

questions.q: Why are adobe homes good in hot places?
questions.a: Thick mud-brick walls keep the inside cool.

days.guide: Sort clothing cards by place.

questions.q: What do people wear in snowy places?
questions.a: Warm coats, boots, mittens, hats.
Light, loose clothing and hats to block the sun.

days.guide: Compare life at the beach, in the Sierra Nevada, and in the desert.

questions.q: A fun winter activity in the Sierra Nevada?
questions.a: Skiing or sledding in snow.

questions.q: What do people need in the desert?
questions.a: Water, shade, sun protection.

days.guide: Compare transportation in snowy places, islands, and cities.

questions.q: How do people travel between islands?
questions.a: By boat or plane.
They move easily over snow.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 assessment.

questions.q: Find California on a U.S. map.
questions.a: On the west coast.

questions.q: How does living near snow affect clothing?
questions.a: People wear warm, waterproof clothes.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test (suggested): 1) Find California on U.S. map 2) Mark the Pacific Ocean 3) Name 4 directions on a compass rose 4) Use a map key to find a park symbol 5) Point to your continent (North America) 6) Explain: people in snowy places wear warm coats and build homes to keep heat in (or similar accurate example). Proficient 5–6 with a clear environment explanation.

weeks.prep: A U.S. flag, printed Pledge of Allegiance, lyrics to 'My Country 'Tis of Thee' (Samuel Francis Smith) and 'America the Beautiful' (Katharine Lee Bates), and photos of American landscapes (mountains, wheat fields, coasts).
misconceptions: Saying the Pledge without knowing the words' meanings: discuss each key word.
Thinking 'indivisible' means invisible: it means cannot be divided — one nation together.
Thinking patriotic songs are only for holidays: they express love for the country any time.

days.guide: Read the Pledge line by line; discuss allegiance, liberty, justice.

questions.a: Loyalty — promising to be faithful.
Freedom.
Fairness.

days.guide: Draw a picture for liberty, justice, indivisible.

questions.a: Cannot be divided; we stay united as one nation.
Example: a balance scale or people being treated fairly.

days.guide: Learn the first verse of 'My Country 'Tis of Thee'; talk about 'sweet land of liberty.'

questions.q: What does 'sweet land of liberty' mean?
questions.a: A country we love where people are free.

questions.q: What is the last line of the first verse?
questions.a: 'Let freedom ring!'

days.guide: Learn the first verse of 'America the Beautiful'; match lines to landscape photos.

questions.a: Golden wheat fields.
Tall mountains that look purple from far away.

days.guide: Your child recites the Pledge, sings one song, and explains one idea.

questions.a: I pledge allegiance to the Flag of the United States of America, and to the Republic for which it stands, one Nation under God, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all.
Example: 'Liberty and justice for all' means everyone should be free and treated fairly.

weeks.assessment_key: Recitation rubric: 4 = recites the Pledge accurately and explains a key word (liberty = freedom; justice = fairness; indivisible = can't be divided; allegiance = loyalty); 3 = 1–2 prompts; 2 = several prompts; 1 = cannot recite.

weeks.prep: Library of Congress photos of veterans, card-making supplies, a children's nonfiction book on the 1621 harvest feast, and 'Thank You, Sarah: The Woman Who Saved Thanksgiving' by Laurie Halse Anderson (library).
misconceptions: Confusing Veterans Day and Memorial Day: Veterans Day (Nov. 11) honors everyone who served; Memorial Day honors those who died serving.
Thinking the first Thanksgiving was only the Pilgrims: the Wampanoag people, led by Massasoit, were there too and had helped the Pilgrims.
Thinking Thanksgiving was always a national holiday: Sarah Josepha Hale worked for years until President Lincoln made it national in 1863.

days.guide: Learn what a veteran is and why we honor them on November 11. View LOC photos.

questions.a: Someone who served in the armed forces.
November 11.

days.guide: Your child writes a thank-you card to a veteran.

questions.q: What could you thank a veteran for?
questions.a: Serving and protecting our country.
A family member, neighbor, or local VA.

days.guide: Learn about the 1621 harvest feast of the Wampanoag and the Pilgrims.

questions.a: The Pilgrims (English colonists at Plymouth) and the Wampanoag people.

questions.q: How had the Wampanoag helped the Pilgrims?
questions.a: Taught them to grow corn and find food (Tisquantum/Squanto helped them plant corn and fish).

days.guide: Read 'Thank You, Sarah'; learn how Sarah Hale helped make Thanksgiving national.

questions.q: How did Sarah Hale try to make Thanksgiving a national holiday?
questions.a: She wrote many letters to presidents and leaders for many years.
Abraham Lincoln, in 1863.

days.guide: Your child makes a two-panel poster explaining Veterans Day and Thanksgiving.

questions.q: What goes on the Veterans Day panel?
questions.a: Honoring people who served in the military, on November 11.
Giving thanks; harvest feast of 1621; Sarah Hale; fourth Thursday of November.

weeks.assessment_key: Poster rubric: 4 = Veterans Day honors people who served in the armed forces on Nov. 11; Thanksgiving is a day of giving thanks, recalling the 1621 harvest feast of the Wampanoag and Pilgrims and Sarah Hale's work (national holiday since Lincoln, 1863); 3 = both correct, few details; 2 = one holiday correct; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Smithsonian/LOC images of the flag, bald eagle, Great Seal (on the back of a $1 bill), Statue of Liberty, and Liberty Bell; construction paper; a quarter dated 1998 or earlier (eagle on back) if available.
misconceptions: Thinking the flag always had 50 stars: stars were added as states joined; there are 13 stripes for the 13 original colonies.
Thinking the Statue of Liberty was built in America by Americans: it was a gift from the people of France (dedicated in 1886).
Thinking the Liberty Bell is still rung: it cracked and is no longer rung.

days.guide: Count stars and stripes; learn their meaning; make a paper flag.

questions.q: How many stars, and what do they stand for?
questions.a: 50, one for each state.
13, for the 13 original colonies (7 red, 6 white).

days.guide: Learn why the bald eagle is the national bird; find it on the Great Seal (back of the $1 bill) and older quarters.

questions.q: Why was the bald eagle chosen?
questions.a: It is native to North America and stands for strength and freedom.

questions.q: Where can you see the eagle?
questions.a: On the Great Seal (on the back of the $1 bill) and on many quarters from 1998 and earlier.

days.guide: View LOC photos of the Statue of Liberty being built; discuss what it welcomes.

questions.q: Who gave the Statue of Liberty to the U.S.?
questions.a: The people of France.
Immigrants and visitors arriving by ship in New York Harbor; it stands for freedom.

days.guide: Find the crack in a Liberty Bell photo and learn its story.

questions.a: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.
It cracked, and the crack grew too large (by the 1840s).

days.guide: Match 6 symbols to names and meanings.

questions.a: Freedom and welcome.
Strength and freedom.

weeks.assessment_key: Matching key: flag — our country (50 states, 13 colonies); bald eagle — national bird, strength/freedom; Statue of Liberty — freedom and welcome to immigrants; Liberty Bell — liberty/independence; Great Seal — official seal of the U.S.; White House — home of the president (if used). Proficient 6/6.

weeks.prep: National Archives (DocsTeach/archives.gov) images of the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution, a magnifying glass, and paper for a family constitution.
misconceptions: Thinking the Declaration and Constitution are the same: the Declaration (1776) said we're free from Britain; the Constitution (1787) set up how the government works.
Thinking George Washington wrote the Declaration: Thomas Jefferson was the main writer.
Thinking July 4th celebrates the Constitution: it celebrates the Declaration of Independence.

days.guide: Examine the Declaration with a magnifier; find John Hancock's signature.

questions.a: John Hancock's.

days.guide: Learn that the Declaration said America would be free; we celebrate on Independence Day.

questions.a: The colonies would be free and independent from Great Britain's king.
Fireworks, parades, picnics, flags.

days.guide: Look at 'We the People' on the Constitution; discuss it as the nation's rulebook.

questions.q: What are the first three words of the Constitution?
questions.a: We the People.
The plan and rulebook for our government.

days.guide: Write a 'family constitution' with 3 rules everyone signs.

questions.a: To show they agree to follow it.
Example: We will speak kindly to each other.

days.guide: Your child explains each document and names one person connected to it.

questions.q: Who wrote most of the Declaration?
questions.a: Thomas Jefferson.

questions.q: Who led the meeting where the Constitution was written?
questions.a: George Washington.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = Declaration — said America would be free from Britain (1776), Jefferson; Constitution — the rulebook/plan for government that starts 'We the People' (1787), Washington; family constitution with 3 signed rules; 3 = mostly correct; 2 = confuses documents; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: 'Martin's Big Words' by Doreen Rappaport (library) and a Library of Congress photo of the 1963 March on Washington. Preview: the book mentions segregation and Dr. King's death in simple terms; be ready to answer questions gently.
misconceptions: Thinking Dr. King used fighting to make change: he taught peaceful protest and words.
Thinking unfair laws were only long ago and everywhere: segregation laws were in many places (especially the South) and changed through the Civil Rights Movement.
Thinking MLK Day is his birthday exactly: it's the third Monday in January, near his birthday (January 15).

days.guide: Read 'Martin's Big Words' and list 3 'big words' Dr. King used.

questions.q: Name some big words from the book.
questions.a: Examples: love, freedom, together, equal.
Equal rights and fair treatment for all people, especially Black Americans.

days.guide: Study the LOC photo of the March on Washington: see, think, wonder.

questions.a: Huge crowds of people, signs, the Lincoln Memorial or Washington Monument.

questions.q: Why did so many people gather?
questions.a: To ask for jobs and freedom and equal rights; Dr. King gave his 'I Have a Dream' speech there.

days.guide: Your child writes and illustrates their dream for a fairer world.

questions.a: I have a dream that everyone is treated kindly no matter how they look.

questions.q: How does it connect to Dr. King?
questions.a: He dreamed of fairness and equality.

days.guide: Role-play solving a disagreement with words.

questions.q: How would Dr. King solve a disagreement?
questions.a: Peacefully, by talking and listening, not fighting.
'I feel... when... Can we...?'

days.guide: Your child tells why we celebrate MLK Day and one thing Dr. King worked for.

questions.a: The third Monday in January.
Equal rights, fairness, peace.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = dream writing connects to fairness/equality and explanation says we honor Dr. King for working peacefully for equal rights (civil rights) on the third Monday in January; 3 = mostly correct; 2 = vague; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Picture biographies of George Washington and Abraham Lincoln (library), a quarter, a penny, a $1 bill, a $5 bill (if available), LOC portraits, and photos of the Washington Monument and Lincoln Memorial.
misconceptions: Mixing up which president is on which coin: Washington on the quarter and $1; Lincoln on the penny and $5.
Thinking Washington and Lincoln lived at the same time: Washington was first president (1789); Lincoln was 16th (1861).
Thinking Presidents' Day honors only current presidents: it honors Washington, Lincoln, and all presidents.

days.guide: Read a Washington biography; list 2 facts; find him on the quarter and $1.

questions.a: George Washington.

questions.q: What did he do before he was president?
questions.a: Led the American army in the Revolutionary War.

days.guide: Read a Lincoln biography; learn why he was 'Honest Abe'; find him on the penny.

questions.a: He was known for honesty — stories tell of him walking miles to return a customer's change.

questions.q: What did Lincoln do as president?
questions.a: Led the country during the Civil War and worked to end slavery.

days.guide: Compare Washington and Lincoln on a Venn diagram.

questions.a: Both were presidents and leaders, both are on money and have memorials in Washington, D.C.
Washington was first president and a general; Lincoln was 16th and led during the Civil War.

days.guide: Match the Washington Monument and Lincoln Memorial to each president.

questions.q: Which is a tall, thin tower?
questions.a: The Washington Monument.

questions.q: Which has a big statue of a seated president?
questions.a: The Lincoln Memorial.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 assessment.

questions.a: Abraham Lincoln.

questions.q: What does the Liberty Bell stand for?
questions.a: Freedom/liberty.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test (suggested): 1) Flag stars = 50 states 2) Stripes = 13 colonies 3) National bird = bald eagle 4) Statue of Liberty = gift from France, freedom 5) Declaration = July 4, 1776, freedom from Britain 6) Constitution = 'We the People,' rulebook 7) Veterans Day honors people who served 8) MLK worked for equal rights 9) Washington = first president, quarter 10) Lincoln = Honest Abe, penny. Proficient 9–10.

weeks.prep: Calisphere/LOC photos of one-room schoolhouses, a small chalkboard or slate, chalk, a picture book about school long ago, and a then-and-now chart.
misconceptions: Thinking children long ago didn't go to school: many did, often in one-room schools with all ages together.
Thinking schools long ago had computers or lots of paper: they used slates, chalk, and a few books.
Thinking everything about school changed: some things stayed the same (reading, writing, math, recess).

days.guide: Study a one-room schoolhouse photo: see, think, wonder.

questions.a: One room, children of many ages, rows of desks, a teacher, a stove, a chalkboard.

questions.q: Why were all ages in one room?
questions.a: Small towns had few children and one teacher.

days.guide: Do spelling on a slate; discuss life without paper.

questions.a: Paper was expensive; slates could be wiped and reused.
You can't keep your work.

days.guide: Make a then-and-now chart.

questions.q: How did children get to school long ago?
questions.a: Walked or rode horses.
Food from home in a tin pail.

days.guide: Read a picture book about school long ago.

questions.q: Name a detail from the book.
questions.a: Answers vary; check the book.
Learning to read, write, and do math.

days.guide: Your child draws themselves at school then and now with 3 labeled differences.

questions.a: Slate then / tablet or paper now.
One room for all ages then / grades now.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = two drawings with 3 accurate labeled differences (slate vs. paper/computer, one-room vs. many grades, walking vs. bus/car, wood stove vs. heaters, lunch pail vs. lunchbox); 3 = 2 differences; 2 = 1 difference; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Calisphere photos of a California main street around 1900 and a historic photo of your own town (Calisphere, local library, or historical society), plus boxes for a model.
misconceptions: Thinking communities were completely different long ago: some things stayed (stores, schools, churches, post offices).
Thinking all photos are 'long ago' if black and white: check dates.
Thinking jobs like blacksmith still exist everywhere: some jobs became rare as technology changed.

days.guide: Look at a California main street around 1900; list same and different.

questions.a: Horses and wagons instead of cars, dirt roads, different clothes.
Stores, people shopping, buildings along a main street.

days.guide: Learn about the general store, blacksmith, milkman.

questions.a: Made and fixed metal tools and horseshoes.
Delivered milk to homes.

days.guide: Find a historic photo of your town; compare with today.

questions.a: Answers vary — e.g., more buildings, paved roads.
Answers vary — e.g., same street, old building.

days.guide: Build a 'long ago' main street from boxes with 3 buildings.

questions.a: Example: general store, blacksmith shop, schoolhouse.

questions.q: What would be on the street?
questions.a: Horses and wagons.

days.guide: Your child explains 2 changes and 1 thing that stayed the same.

questions.a: Cars replaced horses; roads were paved.
People still shop at stores on main streets.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = 2 changes and 1 continuity, each supported by details in the photos; 3 = correct but little photo evidence; 2 = only changes; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: LOC photos of a stagecoach, a steam train, a Model T, and an early airplane; a long paper strip for a timeline; recycled materials.
misconceptions: Thinking cars came before trains: steam trains came first (1800s), then cars (Model T, 1908), then airplanes for travelers.
Thinking travel was always fast: a stagecoach trip took days.
Thinking only fast travel matters: inventions also changed comfort and safety.

days.guide: Sort photos oldest to newest.

questions.q: Order: Model T, stagecoach, airplane, steam train.
questions.a: Stagecoach, steam train, Model T, airplane.
The stagecoach.

days.guide: Create a transportation timeline with drawings.

questions.q: What goes on the left of a timeline?
questions.a: The oldest things.
Airplanes (or today's electric cars).

days.guide: Compare a stagecoach trip and a car trip to San Francisco.

questions.a: The car — hours instead of days.
The car — stagecoaches were bumpy and dusty.

days.guide: Build a wagon or train from recycled materials.

questions.q: What did your vehicle use for power long ago?
questions.a: Horses (wagon) or steam (train).
Wheels, cars/carriage, engine.

days.guide: Your child explains how one invention changed travel.

questions.a: Trains carried people and goods far, much faster than wagons.
Cars let families travel on their own, fast.

weeks.assessment_key: Timeline order: walking/horse and wagon → stagecoach → steam train → early car (Model T) → airplane → today's cars/jets. Proficient = correct order with labels and a sentence about one change.

weeks.prep: A washboard or photo, LOC photos of family life long ago, a jar with a lid and heavy cream (to shake into butter), and 'Ox-Cart Man' by Donald Hall (library).
misconceptions: Thinking chores long ago were easy: they took much more time and effort by hand.
Thinking everyone had appliances long ago: washing machines and refrigerators became common in the 1900s.
Thinking the Ox-Cart Man's family bought everything: they made or grew almost everything themselves.

days.guide: Look at photos of washboards and butter churns; shake cream in a jar until it becomes butter (about 10–15 minutes).

questions.q: How long did it take to make butter?
questions.a: Many minutes of shaking — hard work.

questions.q: How was laundry washed long ago?
questions.a: By hand, scrubbing on a washboard.

days.guide: List appliances that do those jobs today.

questions.a: A washing machine.

questions.q: Where do we get butter now?
questions.a: The grocery store (made in factories).

days.guide: Compare jobs of grandparents' generation with jobs today.

questions.a: Computer programmer, app designer.

questions.q: Name a job that's been around a long time.
questions.a: Farmer, teacher, doctor.

days.guide: Read 'Ox-Cart Man'; list the family's work through the year.

questions.q: What did the father take to Portsmouth Market?
questions.a: Things the family made and grew — wool, a shawl, mittens, candles, shingles, birch brooms, potatoes, apples, honey, maple sugar, goose feathers.

questions.q: What did he sell at the end?
questions.a: The cart and the ox too.
An iron kettle, an embroidery needle, a knife, and peppermint candies.

days.guide: Your child makes a then-and-now chart of 4 household jobs.

questions.a: Washboard by hand / washing machine.
Wood stove or fire / electric or gas stove, microwave.

weeks.assessment_key: Chart: proficient = 4 jobs, each with a correct 'then' (by hand) and 'now' (machine): laundry (washboard → washing machine), butter (churn → store-bought), cooking (wood stove → electric/gas stove), keeping food cold (icebox → refrigerator), cleaning floors (broom → vacuum).

weeks.prep: Marbles, jacks, chalk for hopscotch, a button and string (whirligig), a cup-and-ball (cup, string, ball), and photos of children's clothing from 1900.
misconceptions: Thinking old toys were boring: kids made up many games with simple toys.
Thinking manners are old-fashioned: many manners (please, thank you, shaking hands) are still used.
Thinking children wore the same clothes then: girls often wore long dresses and boys wore knickers.

days.guide: Learn and play marbles, jacks, and hopscotch.

questions.a: Toss a marker, hop through squares on one foot (two in side-by-side squares), skip the marked square.

questions.q: What do you need for jacks?
questions.a: Small jacks and a little ball.

days.guide: Make a whirligig or cup-and-ball.

questions.a: Wind up the string, then pull to make the button spin.

questions.q: What were toys long ago made from?
questions.a: Wood, string, cloth, tin.

days.guide: Compare children's clothing from 1900 and today.

questions.a: Long dresses, aprons/pinafores, high boots.
T-shirts, jeans, sneakers.

days.guide: Discuss manners long ago and which we still use.

questions.a: Bowing or curtsying, saying 'Yes, ma'am.'
Please and thank you, shaking hands.

days.guide: Your child teaches an old game and explains it.

questions.q: How was hopscotch played long ago?
questions.a: On chalk or scratched lines in dirt, same as today.

questions.q: Why did kids play simple games?
questions.a: Fewer toys; games used things they had.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = teaches an old game with clear rules and explains it was played long ago with simple materials; 3 = rules mostly clear; 2 = demo without explanation; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: An interview question sheet (6 questions), a phone/recording device, a grandparent or older neighbor (in person or video), Venn diagram paper, stapled booklet, and then/now picture cards.
misconceptions: Asking only yes/no questions: ask 'What... How... Tell me about...'
Forgetting to listen: let the person finish before asking the next question.
Thinking 'then' means 1,000 years ago: a grandparent's childhood counts as 'then' too.

days.guide: Write 6 questions about school, games, jobs, transportation.

questions.a: Example: What games did you play when you were my age?
They give short answers; open questions give stories.

days.guide: Interview a grandparent or older neighbor; record answers.

questions.q: How do you show good manners in an interview?
questions.a: Say thank you, listen, don't interrupt.

questions.q: What should you do with answers?
questions.a: Record or write them down.

days.guide: Compare their answers with your life in a Venn diagram.

questions.a: Answers vary — e.g., both liked playing outside.
Answers vary — e.g., they had no internet.

days.guide: Make a 'Then and Now' booklet with one fact per page.

questions.a: One fact from the interview with a then/now drawing.
The person interviewed.

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 assessment.

questions.q: Slate or tablet: then or now?
questions.a: Slate = then; tablet = now.
Stagecoach = then; car = now.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test (suggested): sort pictures — then: slate, one-room school, stagecoach, washboard, butter churn, long dress; now: tablet, school bus, car, washing machine, refrigerator, jeans. Explain one change in school, transportation, and family life each. Proficient = 11–12 sorted + 3 explanations. Booklet: 4+ pages with accurate facts.

weeks.prep: Family photos or drawings, a world map, yarn and tape, and paper for drawing a tradition.
misconceptions: Thinking everyone's family looks the same: families come in many shapes and sizes.
Thinking a 'diverse community' means only different languages: it includes foods, traditions, religions, abilities, and ideas.
Sharing family information that's private: share only what your family is comfortable with.

days.guide: Make a simple family tree with photos or drawings.

questions.q: What goes at the bottom (or center) of your family tree?
questions.a: You.
Parents, then grandparents.

days.guide: Find where your family came from on a world map; connect with yarn.

questions.q: Where did your family come from?
questions.a: Answers vary.
The journey from that place to where we live now.

days.guide: Share and draw a family tradition.

questions.a: Examples: a holiday meal, a special song, a birthday custom.
They connect us to family and culture.

days.guide: Visit the library or a farmers' market; note languages, foods, cultures.

questions.a: Answers vary — e.g., people speaking Spanish, Vietnamese; tamales, dumplings.
Having many different kinds of people and cultures.

days.guide: Your child explains one way the community is diverse and one shared value.

questions.a: People speak many languages.
Everyone cares about family and being treated fairly.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = family tree with at least 3 generations (or the family's chosen structure), clear example of community diversity, and a shared value; 3 = mostly complete; 2 = missing explanation; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Calisphere photos of Pomo and Miwok baskets, a map of California tribal homelands (e.g., the California Indian Heritage Center or a library resource), information about the tribe(s) native to your area (e.g., Ohlone, Tongva, Chumash, Miwok), sunflower seeds and two smooth stones.
misconceptions: Thinking American Indians only lived long ago: California Indian nations live, work, and keep traditions today.
Thinking all American Indians were the same: California had many tribes with different languages and ways of life.
Using stereotypes (feather headdresses, teepees) for California tribes: most California tribes lived in homes made of tule reeds, bark, or brush and had their own customs.

days.guide: Learn the tribe(s) native to your area; locate the homeland on a map.

questions.q: Which tribe's homeland are we on?
questions.a: Answers depend on location — e.g., Ohlone (San Francisco Bay Area), Tongva (Los Angeles area), Chumash (Santa Barbara coast), Miwok (central California).

questions.q: Were there many tribes in California?
questions.a: Yes — more than 100 tribes speaking many languages.

days.guide: Examine Pomo and Miwok basket photos; describe patterns and uses.

questions.a: Gathering, storing, cooking (with hot stones), carrying babies, and ceremonies.
They are very finely woven, some with feathers and shells.

days.guide: Learn how acorns became flour; grind sunflower seeds with stones.

questions.q: How were acorns made into food?
questions.a: Gathered, cracked, ground into flour with stone tools, washed (leached) with water to remove bitterness, then cooked as mush or bread.
To remove bitter tannins.

days.guide: Read about California Indian communities today.

questions.q: Do California Indians still live in California?
questions.a: Yes — in many communities, keeping traditions like basket weaving, language, and dance.
Basket weaving, language classes, ceremonies, acorn gatherings.

days.guide: Your child explains two contributions of American Indians to California.

questions.a: Basket weaving art; knowledge of plants and acorn food; place names (e.g., Napa, Yosemite, Tahoe).
Caring for the land, such as controlled burning to keep forests healthy.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = two accurate contributions with evidence (e.g., Pomo basket photos show skilled weaving; acorn grinding shows how they made food from local plants; place names) and names the local tribe; 3 = two contributions, little evidence; 2 = one; 1 = inaccurate or stereotyped.

weeks.prep: 'The Name Jar' by Yangsook Choi (library), Calisphere photos of Angel Island Immigration Station, a world map, and yarn.
misconceptions: Thinking immigrants only came long ago: people still move to California today.
Thinking everyone came through Angel Island: Angel Island (in San Francisco Bay, 1910–1940) processed many Pacific immigrants, especially from China; others came over land or by other ports.
Thinking immigrants must give up their culture: many keep traditions while becoming Americans.

days.guide: Read 'The Name Jar.'

questions.q: Why did Unhei want a new name?
questions.a: She worried classmates couldn't say her Korean name and would tease her.

questions.q: What did she decide in the end?
questions.a: To keep her own name, Unhei (which means 'grace'), and teach others to say it.

days.guide: Look at Angel Island photos; discuss newcomers' feelings.

questions.a: In San Francisco Bay.

questions.q: How did some people feel there?
questions.a: Worried, lonely, scared — some were held for weeks or months and carved poems on the walls.

days.guide: List foods, words, holidays, music immigrants brought.

questions.a: Tacos, sushi, pho, pizza, dim sum.
Lunar New Year, Cinco de Mayo, Diwali.

days.guide: Trace immigrant routes on a world map.

questions.q: How did people come from China?
questions.a: By ship across the Pacific Ocean.

questions.q: How did many come from Mexico?
questions.a: Over land, from the south.

days.guide: Your child tells how one immigrant group helped shape California.

questions.a: Chinese immigrants helped build the railroad and brought foods and Lunar New Year celebrations.
Mexican Americans brought foods, music, Spanish place names, and celebrations.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = names an immigrant group and 2 accurate contributions (e.g., Chinese immigrants built the transcontinental railroad and started Chinatowns; Mexican Americans shaped food, language, music, and holidays); 3 = 1 contribution; 2 = vague; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: 'Lon Po Po' by Ed Young, a public-domain Anansi tale (e.g., 'Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom' / how wisdom spread), 'The Mitten' by Jan Brett (library), and a chart. Preview 'Lon Po Po': the wolf dies at the end, which may scare some children.
misconceptions: Thinking folktales are true stories: folktales are passed down to teach lessons.
Thinking cultures have nothing in common: many folktales share lessons (cleverness, kindness, sharing).
Thinking Lon Po Po is just Little Red Riding Hood copied: it's the Chinese version with its own details.

days.guide: Read an Anansi tale and discuss its lesson.

questions.q: Where do Anansi stories come from?
questions.a: West Africa (the Ashanti people), carried to the Caribbean.

questions.q: In 'Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom,' what happens?
questions.a: Anansi tries to hide all the world's wisdom in a pot at the top of a tree, but it falls and breaks, spreading wisdom everywhere.
No one has all the wisdom; listen to others (even children).

days.guide: Read 'Lon Po Po'; compare with Little Red Riding Hood.

questions.a: A wolf pretends to be the grandmother.
In Lon Po Po, three sisters (led by Shang) trick the wolf themselves by getting him to climb into a basket to the top of a ginkgo tree and dropping him; no hunter saves them.

days.guide: Read 'The Mitten'; identify cultural details.

questions.a: Nicki loses a white mitten; many animals squeeze inside until the bear sneezes and it flies away; Nicki finds it stretched.
Embroidered clothing, Baba (grandmother), village houses, decorated borders.

days.guide: Make a chart comparing the lessons.

questions.a: Be clever and work together; be careful with strangers.
Sharing space / there's always room for one more — until there isn't! (also: take care of your things).

days.guide: Your child explains what folktales tell about a culture's values.

questions.a: What a culture thinks is important, like cleverness, family, or sharing.
Lon Po Po shows children respecting family and being brave and smart.

weeks.assessment_key: Chart: proficient = each tale's culture (Anansi — West Africa/Caribbean; Lon Po Po — China; The Mitten — Ukraine), a correct lesson for each, and one shared value (e.g., cleverness, family, sharing).

weeks.prep: Library books on Lunar New Year, Día de los Muertos, Diwali, Hanukkah, and Kwanzaa; red paper for a lantern; tissue paper for a marigold; paper for drawing a diya and menorah.
misconceptions: Thinking Día de los Muertos is the same as Halloween: it is a time (Nov. 1–2) to remember and honor loved ones who died.
Thinking all celebrations are on the same date every year: some follow lunar calendars and move.
Thinking a celebration belongs only to one country: people celebrate many holidays around the world, including in California.

days.guide: Learn Lunar New Year customs; make a paper lantern.

questions.q: What is in a red envelope?
questions.a: Money, given for good luck.
It stands for good luck and happiness.

days.guide: Learn Día de los Muertos customs; make a paper marigold.

questions.a: An altar with photos, foods, and marigolds to remember loved ones.

questions.q: When is Día de los Muertos?
questions.a: November 1 and 2.

days.guide: Compare Diwali and Hanukkah; draw a diya and menorah.

questions.a: Both are festivals of lights in autumn/winter.
Eight.
A small clay oil lamp lit for Diwali.

days.guide: Chart what the celebrations have in common.

questions.a: Family, special food, light, remembering.
To remember, give thanks, and be together.

days.guide: Your child presents one celebration: when, who, two customs.

questions.a: Late January or February; celebrated by Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese, and other families; red envelopes and dragon/lion dances.
Usually in December; Jewish families; lighting the menorah and playing dreidel.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = names the celebration, when it happens, who celebrates, and 2 accurate customs (e.g., Diwali — Oct./Nov.; Hindus, Sikhs, Jains; lighting diyas, rangoli designs, sweets); 3 = one detail missing; 2 = two missing; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Paper squares, crayons, glue, and a long paper strip to connect quilt squares; a Unit 5 assessment sheet.
misconceptions: Thinking differences always cause problems: differences bring new ideas, foods, and friends.
Thinking language barriers can't be solved: gestures, pictures, and kindness help.
Thinking shared values are rare: most families value fairness, kindness, and family.

days.guide: List benefits of a diverse community.

questions.a: Trying new foods, learning languages, new ideas.
Making friends with people from many backgrounds.

days.guide: Discuss challenges and how kindness helps.

questions.a: Not understanding someone's language.
Smile, use gestures, learn a few words, be patient.

days.guide: Make a paper quilt square showing your family culture; connect with others'.

questions.a: A family tradition, food, flag, or language.
To show many cultures make one community.

days.guide: Write a sentence about values everyone shares.

questions.a: Everyone wants to be treated fairly.
Families love and take care of each other.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 assessment.

questions.a: Basket weaving; acorn foods; place names.

questions.q: What did immigrants bring to California?
questions.a: Foods, languages, holidays, music.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test (suggested): 1) Name a local California Indian tribe (e.g., Ohlone, Tongva, Chumash, Miwok) 2) What were baskets used for? gathering, storing, cooking 3) Angel Island is in San Francisco Bay where many immigrants arrived 4) Name an immigrant contribution 5) Lon Po Po comes from China 6) Name one benefit of diversity 7) Name a shared value. Proficient 6–7.

weeks.prep: Magazine or printed pictures (food, house, coat, toys, candy, haircut, doctor, bread, shoes, car repair), sorting mats, and 'A Chair for My Mother' by Vera B. Williams (library).
misconceptions: Thinking wants are bad: wants are fine; needs come first.
Mixing up goods and services: goods are things you can touch; services are work done for you.
Thinking a need is anything you really want: needs are things required to live (food, water, shelter, clothing).

days.guide: Sort pictures into needs and wants.

questions.q: Is a coat a need or want?
questions.a: A need (clothing for warmth).
A want.

days.guide: Sort into goods and services.

questions.q: Is a haircut a good or service?
questions.a: A service.
A good.

days.guide: List goods and services your family used this week.

questions.a: Milk, shoes, books.
Mail delivery, doctor visit, trash pickup.

days.guide: Read 'A Chair for My Mother'; discuss saving.

questions.q: Why did the family need a new chair?
questions.a: A fire burned their home and furniture.
They put coins in a big jar until it was full.

questions.q: Was the chair a need or want?
questions.a: Mostly a want — but it gave the tired mother a comfortable place to rest.

days.guide: Give the sort quiz.

questions.a: Need.

questions.q: A doctor visit: good or service?
questions.a: Service.

weeks.assessment_key: Sort key (suggested): Needs — food, water, house, coat; Wants — toy, candy, video game, bike. Goods — bread, shoes, toy, apple; Services — haircut, doctor visit, car repair, teaching. Proficient 15–16 of 16.

weeks.prep: Coins (pennies, nickels, dimes, quarters), play store items, price tags under $1, a store flyer, and toys/snacks to trade.
misconceptions: Thinking trading is always easy: you must find someone who wants what you have and has what you want.
Thinking bigger coins are worth more: a dime (smaller) is worth more than a nickel.
Thinking money has always been paper and coins: long ago people used shells, beads, and metal.

days.guide: Trade toys or snacks; talk about problems with trading.

questions.a: The other person must want what you have.
Trading goods or services without money.

days.guide: Learn why money makes trading easier; look at historical coins.

questions.q: Why is money easier than trading?
questions.a: Everyone accepts it, so you can buy what you need without finding a perfect trade.

questions.q: What did people use before coins?
questions.a: Shells, beads, salt, metal pieces.

days.guide: Run a pretend store with price tags under $1; pay with coins.

questions.q: A toy costs 35¢. Which coins could pay?
questions.a: A quarter and a dime (or 3 dimes and a nickel).
2 quarters and a dime.

days.guide: Compare prices of 3 snacks; decide what to buy with 50¢.

questions.q: Snacks cost 25¢, 40¢, 60¢. Which can you buy with 50¢?
questions.a: 25¢ or 40¢ (not 60¢); you could buy only one of them.

days.guide: Your child explains why people use money instead of trading.

questions.a: Money is easier because everyone takes it. In our trading game, I couldn't trade because my sister didn't want my toy.
Buying goods and services.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = two-sentence explanation that money is accepted by everyone so you don't need a matching trade, with barter-game example; correct coin payments in store role-play; 3 = explanation correct, some coin errors; 2 = partial; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Three clear jars labeled Save, Spend, Share; 10 pennies (or chore earnings); 'Bunny Money' by Rosemary Wells (library); and a PBS clip about banks if you can't visit one.
misconceptions: Thinking saving means never spending: saving means putting money aside for something important later.
Thinking you can buy everything you want: choosing one thing means giving up another (opportunity cost).
Thinking banks keep the same coins you gave them: banks keep track of how much you have and keep money safe.

days.guide: Read 'Bunny Money'; track how Ruby's money is spent.

questions.q: What did Ruby want to buy?
questions.a: A birthday present for Grandma.

questions.q: Why did Ruby have less money for the gift?
questions.a: Money was spent along the way on other things, including things Max wanted (like vampire teeth), so the gift had to change.

days.guide: Given 50¢ and items at 20¢, 30¢, 45¢, decide what to buy and what you gave up.

questions.q: Can you buy the 20¢ and 30¢ items together?
If you buy the 45¢ item, what do you give up?
questions.a: Both the 20¢ and 30¢ items (you'd have 5¢ left).

days.guide: Label jars; divide 10 pennies; explain the plan.

questions.a: 5 save, 3 spend, 2 share.
To help others.

days.guide: Visit a bank or watch a clip on how banks keep money safe.

questions.a: Keeps money safe and keeps track of how much you have.
A place at a bank to keep money you're saving.

days.guide: Your child draws a savings goal and figures weeks of saving.

questions.q: A toy costs $5 and you save $1 a week. How many weeks?
questions.a: 5 weeks.
3 weeks (you'd have $6 after 3 weeks).

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = savings goal drawing with price, weekly savings amount, and correct number of weeks (e.g., $6 toy, $2/week = 3 weeks), plus oral explanation of a choice and what was given up; 3 = minor math error; 2 = no plan; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: 'From Wheat to Bread' (library) or similar, simple bread or muffin ingredients, and a PBS clip on how crayons or apples are processed.
misconceptions: Thinking bread comes from the store only: many workers help before it reaches the store.
Thinking one person does all the jobs: workers specialize.
Thinking factories make everything by hand: factories use machines and workers.

days.guide: Learn how wheat grows on a farm and is harvested.

questions.a: With a combine machine that cuts and separates the grain.

questions.q: What part of wheat becomes flour?
questions.a: The grain (seeds/kernels).

days.guide: Bake bread or muffins; list jobs it takes.

questions.q: Name jobs that help make bread.
questions.a: Farmer, miller, baker, truck driver, grocer.
Grinds grain into flour.

days.guide: Watch a PBS clip on processing crayons or apples.

questions.a: Machines and workers make or package goods.

questions.q: Name a step in making crayons.
questions.a: Melting wax, adding color, pouring into molds, wrapping labels.

days.guide: Make a flow chart of workers from farm to store.

questions.q: Order: baker, farmer, grocer, miller, trucker.
questions.a: Farmer → miller → baker → trucker → grocer.
To show the order.

days.guide: Your child explains why people specialize, using bread workers.

questions.a: People get really good at one job, so more goods get made faster.
The farmer grows wheat, the miller grinds flour, the baker bakes.

weeks.assessment_key: Flow chart: farmer (grows and harvests wheat) → miller (grinds flour) → baker (bakes bread) → truck driver (delivers) → grocer (sells). Proficient = correct order with labels and an explanation that specializing makes work faster and better.

weeks.prep: A grocery store visit (or virtual tour), pictures of trucks, trains, ships, planes, a cereal box, and paper and markers for an ad.
misconceptions: Thinking all goods are made nearby: many travel far by truck, train, ship, or plane.
Believing everything ads say: ads are made to make you want to buy.
Thinking cashiers are the only store workers: stockers, butchers, bakers, managers too.

days.guide: Visit a grocery store; list workers.

questions.a: Cashier, stocker, butcher, baker, manager.
Puts goods on shelves.

days.guide: Learn how goods travel.

questions.q: Fastest way to move fresh flowers far?
questions.a: Airplane.

questions.q: How do goods cross the ocean?
questions.a: On ships.

days.guide: Look at cereal box ads; discuss marketing.

questions.q: Why do cereal boxes have cartoons?
questions.a: To get children's attention so they'll want it.
A message that tries to get people to buy something.

days.guide: Design an ad poster for homemade bread.

questions.a: Product name, picture, price, reasons to buy.
Example: Warm, fresh bread — baked with love!

days.guide: Your child explains one job that makes, moves, and sells goods.

questions.a: Baker or farmer.
Truck driver.
Cashier/grocer.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = correctly names and explains a maker (farmer/baker/factory worker), mover (truck driver/train engineer/pilot), and seller (cashier/grocer); 3 = two correct; 2 = one; 1 = none.

weeks.prep: A family chore chart template, thank-you card supplies, and interview questions for a community helper.
misconceptions: Thinking work only counts if it's paid: home work like cooking, cleaning, and caring for family is important unpaid work.
Thinking community helpers are only police and firefighters: librarians, mail carriers, sanitation workers, nurses too.
Thinking chores are only for adults: everyone can help.

days.guide: List work family members do at home and how it helps.

questions.a: Cooking, cleaning, laundry, caring for children.
Keeps the family fed and healthy.

days.guide: Interview a community helper.

questions.a: What do you do every day? How do you help our community?

questions.q: Why do we need mail carriers?
questions.a: To deliver letters and packages.

days.guide: Make a family chore chart; take on a job.

questions.q: Name a chore you can do.
questions.a: Feed the pet, set the table, put away toys.
So everyone knows their job.

days.guide: Write a thank-you card to a worker.

questions.q: What goes in a thank-you card?
questions.a: Greeting, thanks for something specific, closing, your name.
Answers vary.

days.guide: Your child explains why unpaid home work is important.

questions.a: Families need meals, clean clothes, and care to be healthy and happy.
Parents, kids, grandparents — everyone at home.

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric: 4 = chore chart with jobs for each family member, interview notes with 3 answers, and explanation that home work matters because it keeps the family fed, clean, and cared for even though no one is paid; 3 = mostly complete; 2 = partial; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Craft supplies for 6 bookmarks or crafts, price tags, coins, and the year's maps, symbol cards, then-and-now booklet, and culture projects. Prepare the year-end review sheet.
misconceptions: Pricing too high: goods must be priced so buyers can afford them.
Forgetting that a vote decides the plan: majority wins.
Mixing up units at review: sort review items by unit.

days.guide: Hold a family vote (direct democracy) on what goods to make and sell.

questions.q: What kind of democracy is a family vote?
questions.a: Direct democracy.
The choice with the most votes.

days.guide: Make 6 goods; set fair prices under $1; make tags.

questions.a: One that pays for materials and that buyers think is worth it.

questions.q: If bookmarks cost 25¢ each, how much for 2?

days.guide: Hold a family market with coins.

questions.q: You sell a 35¢ item and get 50¢. How much change?
Are you a producer or a consumer when you sell?
questions.a: A producer (seller).

days.guide: Review maps, symbols, then-and-now, culture projects.

questions.q: What do the flag's stripes stand for?
questions.a: The 13 original colonies.
Any of the 7.

days.guide: Give the year-end review.

questions.q: Is a haircut a good or service?
questions.a: Service.
Pacific.

weeks.assessment_key: Year-end review (suggested): label 7 continents and 4 oceans; match symbols (flag—50 states/13 colonies; bald eagle—national bird; Statue of Liberty—freedom, gift from France; Liberty Bell—liberty); sort then/now (slate, stagecoach, washboard = then; tablet, car, washing machine = now); sort goods (bread, toy) and services (haircut, doctor). Proficient 90%+. Market: priced goods, made change correctly.
